chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: The Lincoln Theater and the comedian Bylo
summary: The Lincoln opened in 1926 with vaudeville and Curtis Moseby's pit band; Royal recalls Bylo.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: The Lincoln Theater was opened up in 1926 as a theater that showed a picture and had vaudeville and when it opened up, it had a fellow by the -- Doc Strain brought a show out and with him, his partner was a fellow by the name of Sam Russell. His nickname was Bylo (PHONETIC) and by far, he was the funniest man that I have ever seen in my complete life. All comedians since have tried to in some way copy him. That includes the Redd Foxes with their mugging type thing and everything. But Bylo was one of the original first-class funny men. He would -- he was the type of fellow that would just put his head around the edge of the curtain and mug for five minutes and the people would just fall out of their seats and be rolling in the aisles. He was positively a funny man.
And you saw him at the Lincoln Theater.
Yeah, I think he was part of a team called Bylo and Ashes and that was the first opening of the Lincoln Theater in 1926.
The Lincoln Theater was on Central Avenue and (inaudible).
And the Lincoln Theater lasted a while, 20 or 25 years, didn't it?
Oh, it didn't last quite that long, but --

It's still there now, but it is now a church. But they had shows there up until about 1950. But it never was on the first-class way that it was when it first opened. It was positively a first-class theater, first-run and everything else. They had a pit band that played the show. Curtis Moseby had the band in the show. That was the beginning of his advent as an orchestra leader.
